title: Will Undoubtedly Secure For Us the Entire Business: War Profits into the Customer's Equity
participants: E. I. du Pont de Nemours & Co.
Supreme Court of the United States

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The skim was the war itself, and the Court states its size without comment: du Pont "suddenly found itself engulfed with orders for military explosives from foreign nations later to be allies of the United States in the war, and it had to increase its capacity and plant facilities from 700,000 to 37,000,000 pounds per month at a cost exceeding $200,000,000. Profits accumulated and ultimately amounted to $232,000,000." A fifty-three-fold expansion of capacity, paid for out of orders placed by belligerents before the United States was one.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise was the board seat, and it came before the money. "In 1915, when Durant and the bankers deadlocked on the choice of a Board of Directors, they resolved the deadlock by an agreement under which Pierre S. du Pont was named Chairman of the General Motors Board, and Pierre S. du Pont, Raskob and two nominees of Mr. du Pont were named neutral directors." The supplier's president chaired the customer's board as a neutral party, two years before the supplier bought the stock.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: There is no fog in this record; there is a finding of knowledge, which is rarer. The trial court "expressly found" that "reports and other documents written at or near the time of the investment show that du Pont's representatives were well aware that General Motors was a large consumer of products of the kind offered by du Pont", and that Raskob "for one, thought that du Pont would ultimately get all that business". The parties knew what they were buying and wrote it down, which is why there was a case forty years later.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall is in one sentence of an internal document, quoted by the Supreme Court with its own emphasis. On 19 December 1917 Raskob put a Treasurer's Report to the du Pont Finance Committee recommending a $25,000,000 purchase of General Motors stock, drawing on a $90,000,000 war-era expansion fund of which "about $50,000,000 ... was still in hand". His stated reason: "Our interest in the General Motors Company will undoubtedly secure for us the entire Fabrikoid, Pyralin [celluloid], paint and varnish business of those companies, which is a substantial factor." The purchase was not an investment in a market; it was the purchase of a market.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The whitewash here is forty years of nothing happening, and the Court names the mechanism of it: "Failure of the Federal Trade Commission to invoke § 7 against vertical stock acquisitions is not a binding administrative interpretation that Congress did not intend vertical acquisitions to come within the purview of the Act." The agency with the statute never used it on this kind of transaction; the Government sued in 1949 under a 1914 Act about a 1917 purchase; the District Court dismissed the case; and the Supreme Court reversed in 1957, remanding "for a determination, after further hearing, of the equitable relief necessary and appropriate in the public interest". What relief was eventually ordered is not in this opinion and is not asserted here.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: Section 7 of the Clayton Act 1914 as originally enacted, which the Court held reached "any acquisition by one corporation of all or any part of the stock of another corporation, competitor or not" — vertical as well as horizontal — whenever there was reasonable likelihood of restraint or monopoly in a line of commerce.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The holding that "automotive finishes and fabrics" are a "line of commerce" whose relevant market is "coextensive with the automobile industry" — a definition of the market by the customer's industry rather than the product's, which is the analytic move the case is remembered for.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: War orders generate profits; profits fund an expansion fund; the fund buys equity in the largest consumer of what the expanded plant makes; the equity secures the consumer's orders; the orders justify the plant. The Court traces each link in sequence, and the sequence is the case.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That DuPont and General Motors formed the financial axis of an attempted corporate coup against the United States government in the 1930s — the so-called Business Plot — and that the 1917 stock purchase was a step in it.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: NOTHING IN THE DOCUMENT READ FOR THIS DOSSIER SUPPORTS ANY PART OF THAT, and the dossier says so rather than leaving the title to imply it. United States v. du Pont, 353 U.S. 586, contains no mention of any plot, of Smedley Butler, of the 1934 McCormack–Dickstein committee, or of any political conspiracy; the words "Business Plot" do not appear in it. No source on that subject was located or read, and this dossier asserts nothing whatever about it. The node's original title named it; that title has been replaced, because a title is an assertion. What the record does establish is both narrower and, on its own terms, heavier than the legend, because it is a judicial finding rather than an allegation: a munitions maker took $232,000,000 of war profits, set aside $90,000,000 of it, put its own president in the chair of its largest prospective customer's board as a "neutral" director in 1915, and then in December 1917 bought a 23% stake in that customer on the written reasoning that doing so "will undoubtedly secure for us the entire Fabrikoid, Pyralin [celluloid], paint and varnish business". The Supreme Court held in 1957 that this violated section 7 of the Clayton Act. No coup is needed to make that a closed loop, and no coup is claimed.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: United States v. E. I. du Pont de Nemours & Co., 353 U.S. 586, decided 3 June 1957: a civil action brought in 1949 under § 15 of the Clayton Act to enjoin violations of § 7 arising from du Pont's purchase in 1917–1919 of a 23% stock interest in General Motors, the charge being that the close relationship gave du Pont an illegal preference over competitors in selling automotive finishes and fabrics to General Motors. Held, reversing the District Court's dismissal: the Government proved a violation of § 7, and the cause is remanded for determination of equitable relief. In the Court's narrative: WWI explosives orders forced capacity from 700,000 to 37,000,000 pounds per month at a cost exceeding $200,000,000, with profits ultimately of $232,000,000; $90,000,000 was set aside during the war for continued expansion, which bought the Arlington Works (1915), Fairfield Rubber (1916), Harrison Brothers (1917), Beckton Chemical and Bridgeport Wood Finishing; the 1915 Durant–bankers deadlock was resolved by making Pierre S. du Pont chairman of the General Motors board with himself, Raskob and two nominees as neutral directors; the trial court found du Pont's representatives were well aware General Motors was a large consumer of its products and that Raskob thought du Pont would ultimately get all that business; and on 19 December 1917 Raskob's Treasurer's Report recommended a $25,000,000 purchase, reasoning in writing that the interest "will undoubtedly secure for us the entire Fabrikoid, Pyralin [celluloid], paint and varnish business of those companies". The Court also held § 7 reached vertical acquisitions before its 1950 amendment, and that the FTC's failure to invoke it against them was not a binding interpretation to the contrary.

citations.title: United States v. E. I. du Pont de Nemours & Co. et al., 353 U.S. 586 (argued 14–15 November 1956, decided 3 June 1957) — United States Reports, volume 353
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from the Library of Congress's United States Reports collection (2.0 MB) and read as extracted text. The scan's OCR is cleaner than the 1904 volume but not perfect ("acquistion" for "acquisition" in the syllabus); nothing quoted below turns on a doubtful character. THE CASE: "a civil action brought by the Government in 1949 under § 15 of the Clayton Act to enjoin violations of § 7 of that Act resulting from the purchase by du Pont in 1917-1919 of a 23% stock interest in General Motors. The essence of the charge was that, by means of the close relationship of the two companies, du Pont had obtained an illegal preference over competitors in the sale of automotive finishes and fabrics to General Motors, thus tending to 'create a monopoly' in a 'line of commerce.'" The District Court dismissed; the Supreme Court held: "The Government proved a violation of § 7; the judgment is reversed and the cause is remanded to the District Court for a determination, after further hearing, of the equitable relief necessary and appropriate in the public interest to eliminate the effects of the stock acquisition offensive to the statute." THE WAR, IN THE COURT'S OWN NARRATIVE. The du Pont Company's pre-war expansion programme "was barely started, however, when World War I intervened. The du Pont Company suddenly found itself engulfed with orders for military explosives from foreign nations later to be allies of the United States in the war, and it had to increase its capacity and plant facilities from 700,000 to 37,000,000 pounds per month at a cost exceeding $200,000,000. Profits accumulated and ultimately amounted to $232,000,000. The need to find postwar uses for its expanded facilities and organization now being greater than ever, du Pont continued its expansion program during the war years, setting aside $90,000,000 for the purpose." The Court lists the acquisitions made with it: the Arlington Works in September 1915, Fairfield Rubber in June 1916, Harrison Brothers in March 1917, then Beckton Chemical and the Bridgeport Wood Finishing Company. "Thus, before the first block of General Motors stock was acquired, du Pont was seeking markets not only for its nitrocellulose, but also for the artificial leather, celluloid, rubber-coated goods, and paints and varnishes in demand by automobile companies." THE FINDING ON KNOWLEDGE: the trial court "expressly found that '. . . reports and other documents written at or near the time of the investment show that du Pont's representatives were well aware that General Motors was a large consumer of products of the kind offered by du Pont,' and that John J. Raskob, du Pont's treasurer and the principal promoter of the investment, 'for one, thought that du Pont would ultimately get all that business . . . .'" THE DOCUMENT AT THE CENTRE OF THE CASE: "At this time about $50,000,000 of the $90,000,000 fund was still in hand. Raskob foresaw the success of the automobile industry and the opportunity for great profit in a substantial purchase of General Motors stock. On December 19, 1917, Raskob submitted a Treasurer's Report to the du Pont Finance Committee recommending a purchase of General Motors stock in the amount of $25,000,000. That report makes clear that more than just a profitable investment was contemplated. A major consideration was that an expanding General Motors would provide a substantial market needed by the burgeoning du Pont organization." Raskob's own sentence, quoted by the Court with its emphasis: "Our interest in the General Motors Company will undoubtedly secure for us the entire Fabrikoid, Pyralin [celluloid], paint and varnish business of those companies, which is a substantial factor." HOW THE BOARD SEAT CAME FIRST. "In 1915, when Durant and the bankers deadlocked on the choice of a Board of Directors, they resolved the deadlock by an agreement under which Pierre S. du Pont was named Chairman of the General Motors Board, and Pierre S. du Pont, Raskob and two nominees of Mr. du Pont were named neutral directors." Both men then sat on the Finance Committee, "working closely with Durant in matters of finances and operations and plans for future expansion", and Durant "persistently urged both men and the 'Wilmington people, as he called it,' to buy more stock in General Motors." THE COURT ALSO HELD that § 7 before its 1950 amendment reached "any acquisition by one corporation of all or any part of the stock of another corporation, competitor or not" — vertical as well as horizontal — and that the Federal Trade Commission's failure ever to invoke § 7 against vertical acquisitions "is not a binding administrative interpretation that Congress did not intend vertical acquisitions to come within the purview of the Act." WHAT IS NOT IN THIS DOCUMENT: there is NO mention anywhere in it of any plot against the United States government, of Smedley Butler, of the 1934 McCormack–Dickstein committee, or of any political conspiracy of any kind. The words "Business Plot" do not appear. No source on that subject was read for this dossier, and it asserts nothing about it. Nor does this opinion record what relief was eventually ordered: it remands for "further hearing", and the decree that followed was not read.
